title: Milarepa's songs, two
tomorrow: Mai's project needs a dedication. one person, or everyone?

lines: A WEEK OF WORK, GONE IN SECONDS.
cards: There's a whole kind of video where someone spends a week on a domino run or a sandcastle, and it's gone in seconds. Milarepa's life has a harder version.
Before the cave, tradition says, his teacher Marpa told him to build a stone tower with his own hands. When it was up, Marpa told him to tear it down and carry the stones back. Then build another.
The story has him hauling stone until his back was raw. Later, that same man sings that whatever is built will fall. So why would the tower builder, of all people, sing that?

teach.b: Here's the song's teaching, in plain paraphrase, as his life story gives it. Gathering ends in scattering. Building ends in falling.
Meeting ends in parting. Birth ends in death. Four lines, and none of them is news.
That's the riddle's answer: he isn't guessing.

teach.h: HE LEARNED IT IN HIS SHOULDERS.
teach.b: He learned it in his shoulders. The story says Marpa's towers were a hard training for a man who, before he met his teacher, had done real harm out of revenge.
Building and unbuilding, he found out what everyone finds out late: nothing you raise stays raised. Then listen to what the song does with that.

teach.h: THE SONG DOESN'T DESPAIR. IT TURNS.
teach.b: It doesn't despair. It turns. If building ends in falling, why spend your one life only building?
If meeting ends in parting, meet people now, fully. That's why he went to the cave. Not to escape the world, as he saw it, but to put his life where it wouldn't fall down.
The Pali word for this is anicca: not lasting.
It isn't a threat. It's the weather of everything, including grief, including a bad week.

how: Reflection on impermanence is a common Buddhist practice; in Tibetan traditions it's one of the thoughts students turn the mind with before meditation, and Milarepa's life is often told to illustrate it.

o: work songs that Tibetan builders sang while hauling stone
laments sung at funerals to mourn someone who died
teachings sung in verse, here about everything passing

games.q: the four endings — tap the pairs.

s: impermanence in Buddhism is meant to make you gloomy
the song turns it around: because things pass, spend your life on what matters, and meet people now.
in the story, Marpa made Milarepa build towers and tear them down
tradition says he hauled the stones back and started over, more than once.
Milarepa sang about impermanence from something he'd only read
the riddle's answer: the tower builder learned it with his own hands.

games.q: your friend's band just broke up after two years. she says, 'what was the point if it ended?' what fits the song?
o: it was always going to end, so play it all the way while it lasts
it doesn't matter, nothing lasts, so don't start another band
find a band that will last forever this time
games.why: the song doesn't stop at 'it ends'. it turns: because meeting ends in parting, meet people now, fully.

practice: Find one thing near you that's visibly passing: steam off a cup, light moving on a wall, the rise and fall of your own chest. Watch it change for the whole sit, without wishing it would hold still.

wordCard.voice: Milarepa's songs, again: today, the song of the four endings. Gathering, building, meeting, birth, and where each one goes.

orig.note: Pali: not lasting, impermanent. The first of the three marks of everything that's made.

carryVoice: All things pass, and the man who hauled the stones sang it without bitterness. Two songs down.

sources.ref: The Life of Milarepa (Tsangnyon Heruka): the towers built and torn down for Marpa; the reflection on gathering, building, meeting and birth
The songs of Milarepa: songs on impermanence
